They held the ribbon-cutting at the wellhead itself, which takes a certain kind of nerve — the nerve of a jackal posing for photographs on the kill. The man from Pinnacle Water wore a bolo tie and the slow, courteous, carnivorous smile of a well-fed reptile, and when he said the word stewardship you could smell the rot underneath it, the sweet unmistakable stench of a deal that had died months back and was only now being buried in public, with a band.

By 10:15 the sound system had failed twice, the mayor's drone was tangled in a cottonwood, and a man in a seersucker suit was screaming into a dead microphone about the future in 104-degree heat — the ceremony lurching along, faster and louder, a wild blur of khaki and lanyards and free bottled water drawn from the aquifer whose funeral we had come to attend. "Hey! You can't stand there!" a guard kept howling at Ruiz, my photographer, who was standing on a public county road with a permit.

I asked the guard how deep the new well would go. "1,100 feet," he said, checking his clipboard as if the number were classified. "The old municipal well quits at 400." "And who pays for the casing?" "The district. It's on page 41 of the agreement." "Enemies of the district?" I asked, but he had gone back to guarding the road for $19 an hour, against all enemies, foreign and domestic.

Somewhere on the drive back the idea seized me, arriving fully formed, the way panic arrives, and for ten minutes it was the only sane plan in the county: rent the big water-well rig from the yard on Route 66 — $900 a day, cash, no questions — run it out to the Pinnacle executive golf course at 3:00 a.m., drop the bit through the 14th green, and pump their ornamental lake straight back down into the ground under a hand-painted sign reading RETURN TO SENDER, then be gone before the sprinklers came on, hurtling west with the radio up. Why not? They lift 600,000 gallons a day out of a dying aquifer and call it stewardship; somewhere in the chaos of that arithmetic there is room for one rented rig and one honest gesture.

There used to be a spring at the foot of the mesa, three miles from the new fence line. My grandmother hauled her washing water from it, and cottonwoods grew the whole length of the run, all the way down to the road. The spring is dead now; the trees went one at a time, and the last of them came down in 2009. Nobody planted anything after.

The man from Pinnacle will not be here to see what the land does when the water goes. His kind never is. They feed and they move on, vermin with letterhead, and the ones who stay get the stench and the paperwork and the long, feral, bottomless patience of a doomed little town waiting for rain that comes, when it comes, in March. Watch the fence line; that is where it starts.
